newsitem.title: KENYA: African leaders call for talks to end Zaire war.
newsitem.headline: African leaders call for talks to end Zaire war.

text.p: African leaders called on Wednesday for a negotiated end to the war in Zaire which is tearing apart the continent's third largest country.

Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi told Zaire's prime minister, the presidents of Zimbabwe and Congo, South Africa's deputy president and representatives from Cameroon that failure to end the five-month conflict would have wide repercussions.

"The deteriorating situation in Zaire calls for all our energies to check it to avoid further bloodshed and human suffering," Moi told leaders in Nairobi, including a sombre-looking Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.

"At this stage, and taking into account the latest developments, I can see that a negotiated settlement is necessary in order to arrive at a lasting solution," he added at the opening of a one-day meeting on Zaire.
"It goes without saying that if the crisis in Zaire goes out of hand, the repercussions will be felt far and wide."
The Nairobi meeting followed by one day a disputed Zairean parliament vote in Kinshasa calling for the sacking of Kengo, who was representing his government at the talks in Kenya.
Kengo declined to speak to reporters but officials said he held he was still prime minister despite Tuesday's vote.

The Zairean radical opposition in Kinshasa led by Etienne Tshisekedi sponsored Tuesday's parliamentary motion of censure against Kengo, which also called for a ceasefire and talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
In Kinshasa, a spokesman for Tshisekedi said he would begin contacts soon on forming a government to negotiate with the relentlessly advancing rebels.

Kengo's presence at the summit ended a Zairean government boycott of two previous rounds of talks on Zaire in Nairobi but diplomats expected the meeting to achieve little without the presence of a rebel representative.

In the Zairean rebel headquarters of Goma, rebel information commissioner Raphael Nghenda shrugged off mounting international pressure for a ceasefire and said the Nairobi meeting would not solve anything.
"What counts for us is our people. Although we cannot ignore outside pressure, our people need this war to finish quickly and do not want a ceasefire," he told Reuters in the eastern city.
"The Nairobi summit could only have a very doubtful impact without our presence, and it is clearly not going to produce a serious result when Moi is such a close ally of Mobutu," he added.

U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, visiting South Africa, said he hoped the summit could decide the future of the peace process in Zaire, adding he would personally attend a further summit on Zaire in Lome, Togo on March 26.
South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo told Reuters in Nairobi before the talks opened that South Africa hoped for a ceasefire in Zaire as the foundation of a political settlement.
European Union special envoy Aldo Ajello, attending the meeting as an observer, also called for a ceasefire. The United States and France appealed jointly for a ceasefire on Tuesday.
Mobutu, 66 and Zaire's ruler for 32 years, is being treated for cancer at a hospital in Monte Carlo and has remained in Europe most of the time since the revolt began last October.

Airport officials at Nice in the south of France said Mobutu's plane had arrived and was standing by on Wednesday to take him home. His son and spokesman has said the president was determined to return and make a stand against the rebels.

At the Nairobi meeting were Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, Congolese President Pascal Lissouba, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and representatives of Cameroon, the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
Kabila declared a ceasefire around the captured northeast city of Kisangani from Tuesday and said Kinshasa and diamond mining hub of Mbuji-Mayi in Kasai were the next rebel targets.

In Nairobi, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme said a plane carrying 35 tonnes of food headed to Kisangani on Wednesday to help feed 40,000 displaced people in the city but turned back after receiving a radio message to land at Goma.
